faqs.question: How many games do I need for a 90-minute kids' Halloween party?
faqs.answer: Plan six to eight games and expect to use five or six. Ages 3 to 5 manage 5 to 10 minutes per game, so they get through more; ages 9 to 11 can stay on one strategy game for 20 minutes.

faqs.question: What Halloween games can 3-year-olds play at a party?
faqs.answer: Pick games where nobody is out: passing a soft pumpkin to music, hopping onto paper-plate pumpkins, popping bubbles, or feeling objects through a sock. Keep each to about 5 minutes and give every child the same prize.

faqs.question: How do I stop kids crying when they lose a party game?
faqs.answer: For under-6s, remove losing altogether: no elimination, identical prizes. For 6 to 11, use a group target or personal-best version, and give a child who hates losing a job such as timer keeper.

faqs.question: What are good non-food prizes for a kids' Halloween party?
faqs.answer: Stickers, colouring sheets, bubbles, bookmarks, pencils, temporary tattoos and paper masks all avoid food allergens. Glow sticks, erasers and spider rings suit ages 6 and up but should stay away from under-3s.

faqs.question: How many adults should supervise a kids' Halloween party?
faqs.answer: Our working rule for a home party is one adult per 4 children at ages 3 to 5, one per 6 at ages 6 to 8 and one per 8 at ages 9 to 11, plus a floater who runs no game. That is a host's rule of thumb, not a legal standard.

faqs.question: Can I run Halloween party games in a small flat with no garden?
faqs.answer: Yes. Fourteen of the 20 games here are calm or indoor, and the balloon keep-up or the skeleton hunt can replace an outdoor slot. Tape paper plates flat and move rugs so nobody trips.

faqs.question: Are blindfold games safe for young children?
faqs.answer: Skip blindfolds under 6, because children walk into furniture and some panic in the dark. A feel-through-a-sock guessing game gives the same mystery with eyes open; for older children, clear the floor and keep an adult beside the player.

faqs.question: What should I do if a child gets scared at a Halloween party?
faqs.answer: Turn the lights back up, drop to a calm game and offer a quiet corner with a blanket and an adult for two minutes. Keep costumes and decorations cute rather than gory for under-6s.

faqs.question: Is bobbing for apples a good idea for a kids' party?
faqs.answer: It is a poor fit for 8 to 15 small children: many mouths share one tub of water and young children can inhale it. The games here avoid shared food and water entirely, which also helps children with food allergies.

faqs.question: Can I send a Halloween card to a child who missed the party?
faqs.answer: Yes. SubhSandesh's /happy-halloween page has a Kids mode with round blushing ghosts, no gore and no jump scares, and takes about five minutes to make. It is a one-person greeting, not a party tool, and it is English only.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Party Games for Kids: 20 Games Sorted by Age and Energy

Winning Halloween party games for kids are short, matched to age, and cooperative for the youngest guests: 5 to 10 minutes per game at ages 3 to 5, up to 20 at 9 to 11, alternating loud and quiet. Below: 20 games for 8 to 15 children, with players, minutes, materials, rules, an everyone-wins version and a non-food prize.

Each game fits a phone screen, because 48.3% of SubhSandesh pages are opened on a phone (27,725 of 57,456 views). That figure, like the 11.1 views per page quoted later, is platform-wide, not Halloween data. Then: a 90-minute run sheet, adult ratios and safety rules.

## What makes a party game work for 8 to 15 kids?

A good kids' party game has rules you can explain in 30 seconds, keeps every child playing, and ends before attention does. In a [2025 Frontiers in Psychiatry experiment](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12268353), 120 kindergarteners (mean age 4.73) played one 15-minute fishing game as cooperative or competitive, and the cooperative group shared more stickers afterwards. The effect sat mainly with girls; boys' sharing barely moved.

A [2026 crossover study of 28 children with ADHD](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13053425), in board-game groups of 3 to 4 over 20 days, found cooperative games reduced teasing; stimulant medication did not. Competitive games drew more poor sportsmanship from reward-sensitive children.

## Ages 3 to 5: 7 games with no winners and no small parts

Nobody is ever out and every prize is identical: at this age, elimination ends in tears. Use one adult per 4 children.

### 1. Pumpkin Pass Faces

- **4–15 players, 5 min, calm:** soft toy pumpkin, music.
- **Steps:** Sit in a circle. Pass the pumpkin to music. When it stops, the holder pulls a face. Everyone copies.
- **Prize:** A pumpkin sticker.

### 2. Sleeping Bats

- **6–15 players, 5 min, calm:** a clear rug.
- **Steps:** Children lie still as bats. An adult "owl" tells jokes, never touching. Wrigglers become helper owls.
- **Prize:** A paper bat mask.

### 3. Witch's Sock Drawer

- **4–10 players, 10 min, calm:** 6 socks holding a pinecone, sponge, spoon, cotton wool, mitten, hairbrush.
- **Steps:** Pass one sock round. Each child feels and guesses. Reveal together.
- **Prize:** A ghost colouring sheet.

### 4. Pumpkin Patch Hop

- **6–15 players, 10 min, active indoor:** orange paper plates taped flat, music.
- **Steps:** Dance around the plates. When music stops, hop onto one. Share plates; add more each round.
- **Prize:** Bubbles.

### 5. Spider Web Crawl

- **3–8 at a time, 10 min, active indoor:** wool tied knee-high between chairs, a soft spider.
- **Steps:** Crawl under the web. Rescue the spider. Step back over a low strand.
- **Prize:** A spider bookmark.

### 6. Leaf Pile Treasure

- **6–15 players, 10 min, outdoor:** leaves, 15 tennis balls, a bucket.
- **Steps:** Bury the balls. Dig and fill one shared bucket. Count to 15 together.
- **Prize:** A leaf-print card.

### 7. Bubble Ghosts

- **6–15 players, 5 min, outdoor:** bubble wand.
- **Steps:** An adult blows "ghost" bubbles. Children pop them. The group counts pops to 50.
- **Prize:** A mini bubble bottle.

## Ages 6 to 8: 7 games with an everyone-wins version

Six- to eight-year-olds want to win, so each game adds a group-target version. Use one adult per 6 children.

### 8. Monster Builder Dice

- **4–15 players, 10 min, calm:** paper, crayons, a large foam die.
- **Steps:** Roll for eyes. Roll for arms. Roll for legs. Draw and name the monster.
- **Everyone wins:** Hang every monster in one "museum". **Prize:** A pencil-topper.

### 9. Vanishing Spell Tray

- **4–12 players, 10 min, calm:** tray of 10 Halloween objects, tea towel.
- **Steps:** Study it for 30 seconds. Cover it; remove one object. Name what vanished.
- **Everyone wins:** Whisper to a partner, then answer together. **Prize:** A mini notepad.

### 10. Eyeball Spoon Relay

- **8–15 players, 10 min, active indoor:** ping-pong "eyeballs", spoons, bowls.
- **Steps:** Make teams. Spoon an eyeball to the cauldron bowl. Run back, pass the spoon.
- **Everyone wins:** Teams race their own last time. **Prize:** An eraser.

### 11. Mummy Says

- **6–15 players, 10 min, active indoor:** nothing.
- **Steps:** The leader calls "Mummy says stomp". Moves without "Mummy says" are traps. Anyone caught becomes a helper.
- **Everyone wins:** Helpers stay in play. **Prize:** A temporary tattoo.

### 12. Skeleton Jigsaw Hunt

- **6–12 players, 15 min, active indoor:** paper skeleton cut into 12 bones, tape.
- **Steps:** Hide the bones. Teams search. Tape the skeleton together on a door.
- **Everyone wins:** One skeleton for the whole party. **Prize:** A glow-in-the-dark star.

### 13. Broomstick Slalom

- **6–15 players, 15 min, outdoor:** broom or pool noodle, 5 cones.
- **Steps:** "Ride" round the cones. An adult times each run. Round two, beat your own time.
- **Everyone wins:** Only personal bests count. **Prize:** A witch-hat badge.

### 14. Bat Cave Chain Tag

- **8–15 players, 10 min, outdoor:** cones marking a cave.
- **Steps:** One bat tags. Anyone tagged links arms with the bat. The chain grows until all are caught.
- **Everyone wins:** Everyone ends up on the chain. **Prize:** A slap-bracelet.

## Ages 9 to 11: 6 games with real strategy

Nine- to eleven-year-olds enjoy deduction, codes and tactics. Use one adult per 8 children.

### 15. Haunted Mansion Whodunit

- **4–12 players, 20 min, calm:** 6 clue cards hidden in rooms.
- **Steps:** A ghost "ate the cake". Teams find clues naming monster, room and weapon. Cross off suspects. Name the culprit.
- **Everyone wins:** One team against a 20-minute clock. **Prize:** A notebook.

### 16. Crypt Code Cracker

- **3–12 players, 15 min, calm:** pumpkin-symbol alphabet key, coded message.
- **Steps:** Hand out the key. Teams decode. The message reveals a hidden box.
- **Everyone wins:** The box holds one prize per child. **Prize:** A pencil.

### 17. Crepe Paper Laser Maze

- **6–12 players, 15 min, active indoor:** crepe paper taped across a hallway.
- **Steps:** Cross without snapping a "laser". A snap means restart. Count clean crossings.
- **Everyone wins:** The group target is 10 crossings. **Prize:** A glow bracelet.

### 18. Balloon Bat Keep-Up

- **6–15 players, 10 min, active indoor:** black balloon.
- **Steps:** Stand in a circle. Tap the balloon up. No one taps twice running. Count hits.
- **Everyone wins:** Beat the group record. **Prize:** A keyring.

### 19. Pumpkin Bocce

- **4–12 players, 15 min, outdoor:** 8 small pumpkins, 1 white gourd.
- **Steps:** Toss the white "ghost" gourd. Two teams take turns rolling pumpkins at it. The closest pumpkin scores.
- **Everyone wins:** Both teams' points count toward a shared 12. **Prize:** A mini torch.

### 20. Glow Trail Orienteering

- **6–15 players, 20 min, outdoor at dusk:** numbered glow sticks, 6 letter cards.
- **Steps:** Follow glow sticks to checkpoints. Collect a letter at each. Unscramble the word.
- **Everyone wins:** Teams finish together. **Prize:** A glow stick.

## All 20 games by age, energy and minutes

The three age bands and a mixed-age party, side by side. Numbers match the game headings.

| Age | Games (calm / indoor / outdoor) | Energy split | Minutes per game | Materials |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3–5 | 1–3 / 4–5 / 6–7 | 3 calm, 2 indoor, 2 outdoor | 5–10 | Plates, wool, socks, tennis balls |
| 6–8 | 8–9 / 10–12 / 13–14 | 2 calm, 3 indoor, 2 outdoor | 10–15 | Foam die, spoons, ping-pong balls, cones |
| 9–11 | 15–16 / 17–18 / 19–20 | 2 calm, 2 indoor, 2 outdoor | 10–20 | Clue cards, crepe paper, glow sticks |
| Mixed 3–11 | 1, 4, 7, 12, 18 | 1 calm, 3 indoor, 1 outdoor | 5–15 | Plates, balloon, paper skeleton |

With no yard, 14 of 20 work indoors. The mixed row suits siblings.

## A 90-minute run sheet for 8 to 15 kids

Alternate energy so the room is never loud for over 15 minutes. Food sits at the 45-minute mark:

- **0:00–0:15 Arrival:** a table game (1 or 8) late arrivals can join.
- **0:15–0:30 Active:** two short indoor games (4, 10 or 11).
- **0:30–0:45 Calm:** game 2, 9 or 16.
- **0:45–1:05 Food:** seated, allergy labels on plates.
- **1:05–1:20 Active:** an outdoor game, or 18 if it rains.
- **1:20–1:30 Goodbye:** a costume parade with a named award for every child, then prize bags.

For 12 four-year-olds, that means three game adults plus a floater for toilets, the door and meltdowns. These ratios are our working rule for a home party, not a legal standard.

For tears, offer a blanketed "bat cave" corner and two minutes with an adult. Give a child who hates losing a job, like timer keeper. If the room gets wild, switch to game 2.

## Safety: small prizes, blindfolds and food allergies

The US small-parts rule, [16 CFR Part 1501](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-II/subchapter-C/part-1501) (first published 15 June 1979), bans toys for children under 3 with any part that fits wholly inside its test cylinder. Spider rings, bouncy balls, dice and erasers are that small, so keep them from toddler siblings. Balloons, crayons and modelling clay are exempt, which does not make them toddler-safe.

Skip blindfolds under 6; game 3 uses touch instead. For older children, clear the floor and keep an adult beside anyone with eyes closed.

The [Teal Pumpkin Project](https://www.foodallergy.org/our-initiatives/awareness-campaigns/living-teal/teal-pumpkin-project), adopted nationally by Food Allergy Research & Education in 2014, offers non-food treats in a separate bowl. So every prize above is non-food; ask about allergies on the invitation.

## A Halloween page for the child who couldn't come

SubhSandesh's [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is not a party tool: it is a one-person greeting page that cannot run games, invite a crowd or keep score. It suits the child who missed the party.

Kids mode is spooky-cute: round blushing ghosts, no blood or jump scares, confetti spiders for the trick, and a No button that waits as "maybe later?". Add up to six party photos in about five minutes. Pages average 11.1 views each, and 90.9% of started pages are published (4,724 of 5,199), both platform-wide.

For a 60-second voice note of the party shouting hello, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) suits kids too, with no No button. Both are English only; a handmade card suits a child who doesn't read it.

- Jusko et al., *Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology*, 6 April 2026. [Europe PMC](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC13053425)
- 16 CFR Part 1501, small-parts rule, 15 June 1979. [eCFR](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-II/subchapter-C/part-1501)
- Teal Pumpkin Project, Food Allergy Research & Education. [foodallergy.org](https://www.foodallergy.org/our-initiatives/awareness-campaigns/living-teal/teal-pumpkin-project)

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a reason to cite this over the five pages analysed (Romper, Speech Blubs, Maisonette, SplashLearn, KidActivities): none sorts games by age band and energy, none gives a non-competitive version or allergy-safe prize per game, none has a timed run sheet or supervision ratios, and none mentions the under-3 small-parts rule, Teal Pumpkin practice or any research. The first-party data is platform-wide and only tangential, the ratios are a stated rule of thumb rather than a cited standard, and the domain is far weaker than Romper or retailer blogs, so expect months, not weeks.
